sweep_summary: The single works with stress in the title (Massini-Cagliari 1995, Glottolog 633904) is a Glottolog machine mis-assignment ('computerized assignment from "percurso"') about the history of Portuguese stress — irrelevant to Suruí. The real yield of this search of works with stress in the title is that the previously 'the named source could not be reached' van der Meer 1982 Unicamp thesis (Fonologia da língua Suruí) and the previously 'not located' Guerra 2004 ULB thesis are both fully scanned in the Museu do Índio's DocReader library (app.docvirt.com/mi_bibliografico, folders 8954 and 8677); all 75 + 105 page images were downloaded, scanned (por/eng), assembled into PDFs and with. Van der Meer 1982 pp. 24-30 gives the first-hand stress statement: Suruí is tonal (2 tones) and word stress is free/lexical, normally on a high-tone syllable but not predictable from tone, with the one condition that a stressed final low-tone syllable must be heavy (long or closed); three stress degrees, enclitic-triggered shift to the verb's final syllable, and phrasal rhythmic alternation. Guerra 2004 (tone only) and Surui 2020 (no phonology; cites van der Meer for tone and accent) are silent on stress; Yvinec & Suruí 2017 (LangSci, open) only documents the acute = high-tone orthography. Bontkes 1978 dictionary and Bontkes & Bontkes 1978 phonemic analysis remain unread (SIL archive could not be reached by automated download; Museu do Índio holds only the dictionary's title card), low priority. Language is not in the catalog; van der Meer 1982 p. 28 is the recommended deciding source if it is added.

new_statements.quote: [p. 28] a) Quanto à posição da sílaba acentuada na palavra, esta parece ser livre, com talvez uma única condição para acentuação nas sílabas finais de tom baixo na presença de outras (não proclíticas) de tom alto. Estas parecem só poder ser acentuadas se forem sílabas fortes, isto é, se forem longas ou fechadas. [p. 26] Embora, a nível de palavra, o acento normalmente coincida com sílaba de tom alto, a acentuação é significativa na língua Suruí, não só porque nem sempre esta coincidência se verifica, ou porque há palavras que não têm nenhuma ou têm mais do que uma sílaba de tom alto [...] além de não haver como predizer onde cairá o acento nestas circunstâncias
new_statements.translation: [p. 28] a) As to the position of the stressed syllable in the word, it appears to be free, with perhaps a single condition on the stressing of final low-tone syllables in the presence of other (non-proclitic) high-tone syllables: these seem to be stressable only if they are strong syllables, i.e. long or closed. [p. 26] Although at word level stress normally coincides with a high-tone syllable, stress is significant in Suruí, not only because this coincidence does not always hold, or because there are words with no or more than one high-tone syllable [...] besides there being no way to predict where stress will fall in these circumstances

new_statements.rule_in_words: Suruí is a two-tone language (H/L) with a separate word-stress property. Stress usually sits on a high-tone syllable but cannot be predicted from tone (words may have zero or several H syllables), so its position is lexically free; the p. 28 word list shows initial ('wàlèd 'woman', 'mókòbà 'banana', 'lérég 'skin'), penultimate (mò'kóóbà 'owl') and final (ká'lár 'macaw', yí'bòr 'coati', màkò'bá) stress on comparable words. One weight restriction: a final low-tone syllable can bear (lexical) stress only if heavy (long vowel or closed). Bontkes 1988:123 agrees that stress 'generally falls on one of the high tones of a word' but claims it has no lexical function. If coded for placement alone this is lexical/unpredictable stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described. Van der Meer distinguishes three degrees: 0 (unstressed), 1 (lexical word stress) and 2 (the sentence's phonological nucleus, i.e. the stressed syllable of the predicate verb/ideophone; p. 26-27). Verbs of 3+ syllables followed by enclitics show two stresses (lexical + shifted final), the last being the sentence nucleus (p. 27). Bontkes 1988 notes one doubly stressed noun 'íka'bí: 'mortar', possibly a compound.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitics are excluded from the count of H syllables; stress moves to the verb's (or ideophone's) final syllable before aspect enclitics and before the auxiliary -jé (p. 27, 30); rhythmic re-adjustment to alternating stressed/unstressed syllables inside verbal (OV, V-particle-V), genitive and intensified-verb phrases (p. 29); stress that arises from these shifts is exempt from the weight condition (p. 28). Bontkes 1988: long prefixes toy-/mey- sound stressed in isolated words; in L-L disyllabic roots stress may be on either syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress (degree 1) is stated for words (isolated citation forms in the p. 28 list); degree 2 and the shifts are phrase/sentence phenomena. Intonation not studied (note 2, p. 30). Data: Paiter Suruí of Rondônia, SIL fieldwork, 1970s-1982.
new_statements.identity_note: Paiter Suruí of Rondônia (suru1262, ISO sru, Tupian/Mondé). All sources read (van der Meer 1982, Bontkes 1988, Guerra 2004, Surui 2020, Yvinec 2017) describe this same variety from the same SIL-era community. Not to be confused with Suruí do Pará / Aikewara (ISO mdz, Tupi-Guarani), which is what the SIL item 'Suruí Sevacava' (archive 86319) and Museu do Índio 'Suruí' hits for Pará concern.

new_statements.reading: Suruí (Paiter) is a two-tone language in which word stress is a separate, lexically FREE (unpredictable) property: it usually coincides with a high-tone syllable but cannot be predicted from tone (p. 26: 'não haver como predizer onde cairá o acento'); the only restriction is a weight condition on stressed final low-tone syllables (must be long or closed). Stress has three degrees, shifts to the verb's final syllable before enclitics, and undergoes rhythmic alternation within genitive/verbal phrases (pp. 27-30). The p. 28 word list shows initial, penultimate and final stress on otherwise comparable words. For a catalog's classification this is 'lexical/free stress (tone-correlated), with a weight condition on final syllables' — not a fixed-position system. Verified against the page image; scanned text also.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.quote: p. 54: "Surui language has two phonological level tones, high (H) and low (L). The TBU (tone bearing unit) in Surui is the vowel. There is one tone per vowel, no matter its length, consequently a vowel cannot bear two tones, creating contours ... As each syllable has one vowel only, the number of tones per word is the same as the number of vowels and the number of syllables of that word."
sources.locator: Ch. 4 'Tone', §4.1 p. 54 (scan p058); table of contents p. iv (scan p004)
sources.note: Silent on word stress: the whole thesis (vowels, consonants, tone phonology/phonetics, tone processes) never uses the words 'stress' or 'accent' (0 scanned hits over 105 pages; TOC has no stress section). It describes a two-level tone system with pitch measured on whistled and spoken monosyllables/disyllables and tone dissimilation rules. Does not engage van der Meer's stress analysis.
